fixes.answer: I consider them absolutely essential to a healthy city. Public spaces like parks provide vital areas for recreation, exercise and relaxation, which is crucial for physical and mental wellbeing amid the stress of urban life. They also act as the [[lungs of a city]], improving air quality, and serve as places where the community comes together. So far from being a luxury, well-designed public spaces are fundamental to a [[liveable]] and [[cohesive]] city.
fixes.why: 'fundamental' is plain; marked the idiom 'lungs of a city'

fixes.answer: In many rapidly growing cities, unfortunately not. As urban land becomes increasingly valuable, green and public spaces are often sacrificed for commercial or residential development, which I find [[short-sighted]]. Older, well-planned cities tend to have generous parks, whereas newer, denser developments frequently lack them. So while the importance of public space is increasingly recognised, in practice many cities are [[falling short]], prioritising profit over [[liveability]].
fixes.why: 'short' is part of an idiom and 'profit' is plain; marked 'short-sighted' and 'falling short'

fixes.answer: The effects are overwhelmingly positive, in my view. Access to green spaces reduces stress, improves mood and encourages physical activity, benefiting both mental and physical health. They provide a [[peaceful escape]] from the noise and concrete of the city. Socially, they [[foster]] community interaction. Environmentally, they cool cities and clean the air. So green spaces have a genuinely [[restorative]] and beneficial effect on urban wellbeing.
fixes.why: 'beneficial' and 'wellbeing' are plain; marked 'peaceful escape' and 'foster'; softened 'well-researched'

fixes.answer: Public spaces act as vital social hubs. Parks, squares and community centres provide neutral, accessible places where people from [[all walks of life]] can meet, interact and [[mingle]], whether at a market, a festival or simply while relaxing. This casual contact builds a sense of community and belonging, and helps break down social barriers. In an increasingly isolated world, these shared spaces are crucial for fostering [[social cohesion]] and mutual understanding among diverse people.
fixes.why: 'understanding' and 'diverse' are plain; marked 'all walks of life', 'mingle', 'social cohesion'

fixes.answer: I am hopeful there will be more, though it faces real pressure. On one hand, [[intense competition]] for urban land threatens existing spaces. On the other, there is a growing recognition of their importance for wellbeing and sustainability, and many [[forward-thinking]] cities are now actively creating parks, green roofs and pedestrian zones. So the outcome depends on planning priorities, but I am optimistic that the value of public space will increasingly be recognised and [[prioritised]].
fixes.why: only 2 marks and 'recognised' is plain; marked 'intense competition' and 'forward-thinking'

fixes.answer: Creativity is key when land is scarce. Cities can [[repurpose]] [[disused]] areas, such as old railway lines turned into elevated parks, or convert rooftops into green spaces and gardens. Pedestrianising streets reclaims space from cars for people. Even small pocket parks on vacant plots make a difference. So even in dense cities, with imaginative planning, it is possible to integrate valuable public and green space into the existing [[urban fabric]].
fixes.why: 'planning' and 'integrate' are plain; marked 'repurpose', 'disused' and the phrase 'urban fabric'

fixes.answer: While the benefits are enormous, there are a few considerations. Large public spaces are expensive to create and maintain, requiring [[ongoing public funds]]. If poorly designed or managed, they can sometimes attract [[antisocial behaviour]] or feel unsafe. They also take up valuable land that could be used for housing. However, in my view, these drawbacks are minor and [[manageable]] compared to the immense social, health and environmental value such spaces provide.
fixes.why: 'value' and 'provide' are plain; marked 'ongoing public funds' and 'antisocial behaviour'

fixes.answer: I understand the argument given the housing crisis, but I largely disagree with sacrificing parks. While housing is undeniably crucial, green spaces are equally vital for residents' health and wellbeing, and destroying them creates a poorer quality of life. It should not be an either-or choice. With clever planning, cities can build housing on [[brownfield sites]] and increase density elsewhere while preserving parks. So both are essential, and [[pitting them against]] each other is a [[false dilemma]].
fixes.why: 'preserving' is plain and 'false dilemma' was split; marked 'brownfield sites', 'pitting them against', 'false dilemma'
